sections.section_title: Recognizing Monogenic Diabetes in a Young Adult
sections.description: This section introduces the clinical problem of early-onset diabetes that does not fit neatly into type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Using the patient’s presentation, it teaches learners how to identify clues that should raise suspicion for MODY, especially HNF1A-MODY, and places the case in the broader context of monogenic diabetes.
subtopics: Definition of MODY as an autosomal dominant, non-autoimmune monogenic diabetes syndrome
Epidemiology of MODY and why it is frequently underdiagnosed
Major MODY genes and why HNF1A-MODY is one of the most common subtypes
Typical age of onset, inheritance pattern, and phenotype of HNF1A-MODY
Case presentation: incidental hyperglycaemia and glycosuria on annual examination
Symptoms at presentation: thirst, increased appetite, and weight loss without diabetic ketoacidosis
Physical findings that argued against classic insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes, including absence of acanthosis nigricans and only modest BMI elevation
Family history across multiple generations as a key clue to autosomal dominant diabetes
Why early-onset diabetes with preserved endogenous insulin secretion should trigger consideration of MODY
Common reasons patients with MODY are initially mislabeled as type 1 or type 2 diabetes

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology and Clinical Features of HNF1A-MODY
sections.description: This section provides the targeted background science needed to understand the case. It explains the biology of HNF1A, how pathogenic variants impair beta-cell function and renal glucose handling, and how these mechanisms produce the patient’s biochemical and clinical phenotype.
subtopics: Structure, genomic location, and tissue expression of the HNF1A transcription factor
Role of HNF1A in pancreatic beta-cell gene regulation
Mechanisms by which HNF1A mutations reduce insulin secretion, including effects on insulin, GLUT2, and pyruvate kinase pathways
Progressive beta-cell dysfunction as the basis for worsening hyperglycaemia over time
Why HNF1A-MODY often shows marked postprandial hyperglycaemia before severe fasting decompensation
Renal effects of HNF1A dysfunction and the reduced threshold for glycosuria
Relationship between HNF1A and SGLT2 expression in renal tubules
Clinical phenotype overlap with type 1 and type 2 diabetes and why this creates diagnostic ambiguity
How obesity, dyslipidaemia, or metabolic syndrome features can coexist and obscure recognition of MODY
Genotype-phenotype diversity in HNF1A-MODY and the significance of variants in the DNA-binding domain

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup and Clinical Reasoning: From Hyperglycaemia to Genetic Diagnosis
sections.description: This section walks through the investigation sequence and the diagnostic reasoning used in the case. It emphasizes how clinicians integrate glucose data, C-peptide, autoantibodies, family history, and genetic testing to distinguish HNF1A-MODY from type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

Clinical significance of the absence of diabetic ketoacidosis at presentation
Assessment of endogenous insulin secretion with the glucagon stimulation test
How fasting and stimulated C-peptide values support preserved but impaired beta-cell function
Use and limitations of C-peptide in differentiating MODY from early type 1 diabetes
Role of islet autoantibodies including GADA and IA-2A in excluding autoimmune diabetes
Ancillary findings in the case: lipid abnormalities, absence of microalbuminuria, and reduced sudomotor function
Building the differential diagnosis: type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, and monogenic diabetes
Clinical features that favored MODY over type 1 diabetes
Clinical features that favored MODY over type 2 diabetes despite elevated triglycerides and BMI of 24.6 kg/m2
Usefulness and limitations of MODY prediction tools such as the Exeter MODY probability calculator
Indications for molecular testing in suspected MODY
Next-generation sequencing panels in monogenic diabetes evaluation
Interpretation of the novel HNF1A c.809A>G, p.N270S variant using ACMG principles
Evidence supporting pathogenicity: novelty, domain location, segregation with family diabetes, and in silico support
Why genetic confirmation changes diagnosis from phenotypic diabetes classification to precision diagnosis

sections.section_title: Therapeutic Strategy and Precision Management in HNF1A-MODY
sections.description: This section explains the treatment decisions in the case, starting with empiric therapy before genetic confirmation and then showing how the diagnosis of HNF1A-MODY altered management. It teaches evidence-based pharmacologic choices, treatment goals, and medication-specific considerations unique to this subtype.
subtopics: Initial need for glycaemic control in a patient presenting with HbA1c 10.2% and marked hyperglycaemia
Rationale for starting basal insulin, metformin, and saxagliptin before genetic results were available
Balancing immediate metabolic control with evolving diagnostic uncertainty
Lifestyle treatment: structured diet, exercise, and outpatient follow-up
Standard first-line pharmacology for HNF1A-MODY: low-dose sulfonylureas and their mechanism
Why insulin can sometimes be avoided or discontinued after correct diagnosis of HNF1A-MODY
Reasoning for switching from insulin to GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy after genetic confirmation

Advantages of GLP-1 receptor agonists, including effective glucose lowering with less hypoglycaemia risk
Role of metformin and DPP-4 inhibition as adjunctive or maintenance therapy in selected patients
Interpretation of the patient’s response: HbA1c improvement after one month and after six months
Therapeutic individualization based on residual beta-cell function, glycaemic trajectory, and tolerability
Why SGLT2 inhibitors may be risky in HNF1A-MODY because of glycosuria, dehydration, and ketoacidosis concerns
Principles of precision medicine in monogenic diabetes: matching treatment to genotype and physiology

sections.section_title: Follow-up, Prognosis, and Broader Clinical Lessons
sections.description: This section covers the patient’s outcome, long-term monitoring, and the broader implications of the case for clinical practice. It emphasizes complication surveillance, family implications, and the importance of expanding awareness and genetic detection of MODY.
subtopics: Outcome in this case: sustained HbA1c reduction to 6.0% and maintenance below 6.5%
Monitoring for microvascular complications, including nephropathy and retinopathy
Interpretation of the absence of microalbuminuria and retinopathy early in follow-up

Long-term natural history of HNF1A-MODY and progressive beta-cell decline
How accurate diagnosis informs prognosis and future treatment adjustments
Family screening and genetic counselling in autosomal dominant diabetes

Role of next-generation sequencing in improving detection, cost-effectiveness, and precision care
Core take-home lessons for trainees: when to suspect MODY, when to order genetic testing, and how diagnosis changes management
